title: Land taken before payment for the Bajkaj landfill
place: Palavli village, Vergo, Delvine district, Vlore region, Albania

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Project P086807, Integrated Coastal Zone Management and Clean-up Project. IDA credit 40830, credit agreement C4083-AL conformed 29 June 2005. Approved 21 June 2005, effective 29 November 2005, closed 31 March 2015 after four restructurings. The land acquisition completion report of October 2014 says the landfill was financed by the IDA credit, a grant from the Austrian Government and the Albanian Government. The completion report of 27 April 2016 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, the risk to the development outcome Substantial, and quality at entry Moderately Unsatisfactory.

companies.name: Expropriation Commission, Ministry of Public Works and Transport
companies.role: The unit inside the line ministry that checked ownership titles, issued the expropriation notice to owners and to the press, received grievances and sent the expropriation proposal to the Council of Ministers. Payments were later handled by the Expropriation Commission of the Ministry of Urban Development and Tourism (land acquisition completion report, October 2014).

companies.name: Delvina Municipality
companies.role: The local authority named in the plan as the beneficiary of the expropriation under Albania's expropriation law, and the body that had to submit the request to the line ministry.

community: The landfill at Bajkaj-Palavli needed 3.23 hectares of land. The land acquisition completion report of October 2014 says that covered 21 plots belonging to 20 owners, that the land was used for livestock grazing, and that there were no houses or other structures on it. Its Table 1, headed as per the resettlement plan, names every owner with the size of the plot and the area taken, and a second table repeats the same totals with the number of plots corrected. Four plots were taken in full: Sinan Kuci 892 square metres, Ago Kuci 1,859, Nedin Kuci 2,349 and Shahin Haderi 7,123. In total 32,320 square metres were taken out of 54,235. The report says the land should have been acquired before construction started and was not: "the contractor accessed the land before compensations were paid, which caused tensions, consequently work stoppages at the landfill site from November 2013 to February 2014." It also says the delay came from administrative requirements, including the duty on owners to produce full proof of title, and that the number of plots and the land area first recorded did not match the final figures, so the Council of Ministers had to amend its expropriation decision. Payments were made in early February 2014 after that amendment and the works resumed in mid-February. Total compensation was estimated at 19,547,136 lek, about US$193,920; the report's payment table, dated as of January 2015, lists 15,055,387 lek paid. As of October 2014, 13 of the 20 owners had been paid in full. The report gives two accounts of the remaining seven in the same document: the executive summary says they are "either deceased or living abroad, mostly in Greece", and section 3.2 says seven owners "have not applied for compensation", with migration the reason for three and the death of the proprietor for four. The money for those cases was placed in an escrow account and the report says one family was finalising an inheritance procedure to become eligible. Two further owners were identified as affected by the access road. The report's own monitoring table says the affected people were not dependent on the land, so their incomes were not adversely affected, and that there were no new complaints or community opposition. Three commitments to the villages were recorded as finished in 2014: the road from Bajkaj to Palavli, the two village squares and their entrance roads, and an upgrade of the water supply.
outcome: The Bank's completion report of 27 April 2016 says that at project closure in March 2015 there were no outstanding social safeguards issues and that the compensation question "was resolved before the project closure date". Its safeguards annex gives different numbers from the borrower's report: it says the acquisition took 3.2 hectares "from 21 project-affected people", that full payments were made in 13 cases, and that in 8 cases the people were deceased or living abroad. The borrower's report of October 2014 gives 20 owners, 13 paid and 7 outstanding. The same annex says a resettlement plan for the landfill construction "was prepared and implemented in compliance with World Bank operational policy (OP 4.12)", and that there had been no new complaints or community opposition to the landfill since April 2014. The landfill was 90 per cent built in October 2014 and the works were completed. The report's payment table lists 13 plots paid and 8 unpaid; two of the unpaid plots carry the same owner's name.

title: Orchard cleared and a school built on claimed land, Shkodra and Lezha
place: Mark Lula neighbourhood, Shkodra, Albania, and Lezha

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Project P078933, Education Excellence and Equity Project. IDA credit 41800, XDR 10.50 million committed and XDR 9.83 million disbursed. Approved 1 June 2006, effective 4 October 2006, closed 30 June 2013 against an original closing date of 31 December 2010; restructured 19 March 2010 and 22 March 2012. The restructuring required the recipient to apply the resettlement policy framework retroactively to expropriation already carried out for school construction at Shkodra and other sites, and the amended financing agreement set 30 April 2010 as the date by which the affected party at Shkodra had to be compensated. The completion report of 28 March 2014 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and quality at entry Moderately Unsatisfactory. The European Investment Bank and the Council of Europe Development Bank co-financed the wider programme.

companies.name: Ministry of Education and Science
companies.role: The line ministry that ran the project, wrote the resettlement policy framework and the site plans, carried the expropriation files to the Council of Ministers, and was responsible for paying compensation out of the state budget.

companies.name: Municipality of Shkodra
companies.role: The city government that planned the new school on the site and ordered the demolition of what stood on it.

community: The project was not meant to build new schools. The completion report of 28 March 2014 says it became non-compliant with the Bank's resettlement policy in 2008, when it was found that the Bank had approved government investments in new school construction that the financing agreement did not allow. Its safeguards annex says: "Complicating matters, in June 2008, the Municipality of Shkodra ordered demolition of a 5,000 M2 orchard in anticipation of a contract for new school construction. The Municipality alleged that the orchard was public land being used informally by a private individual." The same paragraph says that no new construction had actually begun under the project when the discrepancy was discovered, and the Shkodra site plan says the project did not originally involve the resettlement policy because no new school construction had been contemplated when it was prepared. At the Bank's request the ministry stopped all work on new school construction and agreed to apply the resettlement policy retroactively and take remedial action for the affected party. The site plan of 15 April 2010 gives the detail and a different month. It says that in May 2008 the municipality "demolished the existing improvements on the parcel and removed the agricultural activities being conducted by a local resident". The resident, whose name the plan withholds to protect his privacy, had used the site as a garden for fruit and grapes since the 1990s. The plan says he had built an enclosure of about 4,000 square metres with a concrete-block wall about 2 metres tall and an iron gate, that about 3,600 square metres was planted with grapes and 400 with cherries, that the vines were supported by trellises hung from concrete poles, and that there was a small toolshed on a concrete platform. He used the fruit to make raki and for sale. He went to court in 2008 to establish that the parcel was his; the Shkodra District Court decided in his favour and the Appeals Court overturned that in April 2009, on the ground that his document referred to land in a different neighbourhood. The plan concludes that the state owns the land and he has no legal or legalizable claim, so the policy requires no payment for the land itself, but does require payment for the assets removed, calculated on five years of production and sale of fruit and raki. The amount is withheld from the disclosed version. The plan's own footnotes cut the other way: they estimate he "did not earn more than 5-10% of his annual income from the garden", note that he "still operates a large garden at the site adjacent to his home, a few meters away from the site of the demolished garden", and say the income estimate assumed full retail prices when he consumed or gave away much of the produce. His house was across an alleyway and was not affected, and the plan says he filed no complaint about the amount offered. The completion report says the ministry met the compensation covenant by May 2010. A second site went the same way. The completion report says that in June 2010 the Bank received a complaint that part of the extension of the 9-Year Beslidhja school in Lezha was being built on land restituted to a family, that the Bank asked for all work on that site to stop until the matter was resolved, and that the municipality then decided to expropriate. The ministry's team found that the Hafizi family owned 873 square metres of the land the school stood on. An agreement signed on 1 November 2010 recognised their ownership and allowed the works to resume. The plan of February 2011 values the land at 20,000 lek per square metre, 17,460,000 lek in all, divided between eight named co-owners in shares from one twelfth to one third. The plan says none of the owners lived on the land, had built on it or had cultivated it. The completion report says "ultimately the land owner was fully compensated for the value of the land". A third problem was left unresolved. The completion report says that in 2013 the Bank was told that a small structure next to the Mar Lulaj school in Shkodra, taken to be municipal property due for demolition as part of the school works, was being claimed by a third party. The report says the municipality "closed access to the structure by walling it off to students", that "it was confirmed that the municipality remains in compliance with safeguards policies, although the legal situation of this structure has not yet been clarified", and that if the claim were confirmed the municipality was expected to begin expropriation. It then says: "The contractor, under instructions from the municipality, constructed a wall that prevented access to the structure, and the Bank requested that this be corrected. As of project closing, the current status of this issue was unclear."
outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2013. The Shkodra compensation was paid by May 2010 and the Lezha owners were compensated for the value of their land. The completion report says the closing date was extended in part to make up "the 23-months it took to resolve the safeguards issues", and that two of the schools, Mar Lulaj in Shkodra and Keneta in Durres, were still not finished when the project closed. The claim over the walled-off structure beside the Mar Lulaj school was unresolved at closing.

title: A Judge Ordered a Family Out of the Road Line Before the Colonia Santa Rosa Access Was Built
place: National Route 34 near the junction with National Route 50, at the access to Colonia Santa Rosa, Argentina; the remedial action plan places the case in the province of Jujuy, near the Bolivian border, while the town of Colonia Santa Rosa is in the Orán department of Salta

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: National Highway Asset Management Project, second phase (P095569), Loan 7473-AR, four hundred million dollars, agreement dated 27 June 2008 with the Argentine Republic. The completion report of 28 March 2014 says the Involuntary Resettlement policy was not activated at appraisal because the works were expected to stay inside existing rights of way where no resettlement was expected, and that the policy had not been triggered on the first phase either. It then says that "activities under the project prompted the Bank to activate six safeguards policies, namely: The Natural Habitats (O.P 4.04), Forest (OP 4.36), Pest Management (OP 4.09) Physical Cultural Resources (OP 4.11), Indigenous People (OP 4.20) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP 4.10)"; the last two numbers are the wrong way round against the Bank's own numbering, in which 4.10 is Indigenous Peoples and 4.12 Involuntary Resettlement, and the evaluation review of 5 November 2014 repeats the same list with the same numbers. The project was restructured in February 2012 to add the policies and the loan agreement was amended. The report says of those impacts that "The impacts were minor, however". The evaluation review says the land acquisition arose because "a few CREMA Contracts (or Mallas) required land acquisition because of temporary dislocation of settlement within the right of way", for roundabouts built as road safety improvements. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and so does the review. The review says "The ICR does not report on the compliance of these policies" and that the project team afterwards informed the evaluation group about compliance, which is a staff statement and not a document.

companies.name: Dirección Nacional de Vialidad (DNV)
companies.role: The national roads directorate of Argentina, inside the public works ministry, which ran the project and the CREMA rehabilitation and maintenance contracts. The remedial action plan lists the steps DNV was to take on each case, with deadlines, including obtaining the land and opening expropriation proceedings where owners would not agree. The completion report says it took DNV a while to grasp, internalise and accept what it calls the unexpected requirements from the Bank.

community:
The remedial action plan filed under this loan on 7 December 2011 lists eight cases under the World Bank's involuntary resettlement policy where the project's road works had run into land the roads directorate did not own. In four of the eight the plan states that the works had already been carried out, one was dropped when the project was reformulated, two are marked for future relocation and one has no affected party listed.

The case with people in it is on National Route 34 near the junction with National Route 50, at the access road to Colonia Santa Rosa. The plan names a family that ran a comedor, a canteen, in the line of the road until 2009, and the owner of a depot who occupied the right of way. Its footnote sets out what happened: the canteen operator was served with judicial notice in 2002 that he was in the right of way, a judge ordered his eviction in 2009, and he moved to Saucelito with the support of the municipality. The plan says the works had already been done, and the step still owed to the World Bank was for the roads directorate to send a report from the municipality of Colonia Santa Rosa documenting the relocation of the family that ran the canteen and the measures taken to compensate or support the owner of the depot. A second footnote records that the depot owner is the widow of the man originally sued.

Two further cases on the same route, at the accesses to Embarcación and Aguaray, concern informal occupants of the right of way and a restaurant. The plan marks both for future relocation and requires an abbreviated resettlement plan to be sent to the Bank four months before construction of the access begins.

The other cases are land the works crossed without acquiring it from companies and a municipality: parcels of the oil company YPF at two places in Chubut, where the plan says the works had been done and the roads directorate was to obtain the land by agreement or begin expropriation proceedings, and land of a sugar company near the Calilegua National Park in Jujuy, where a new bridge and an access had been built and the works were still to be declared of public utility. One case in Jujuy was dropped when the works were reformulated.

A separate section covers the Bank's indigenous peoples policy: the rehabilitation and maintenance of a road in Neuquén affects the Namuncurá, Cayulef, Paineo and Cayupan communities, and the plan says those works had not yet been carried out and a plan for indigenous peoples existed in draft, based on a preliminary consultation with the affected communities.
outcome: The project closed on 30 September 2013, having been due to close on 31 December 2011. The completion report says the documents that are generally needed, a resettlement and remedial action plan and a framework for indigenous peoples, had now been drawn up during this project, and that the safeguards issue caused frustration among the roads directorate's staff and disruption to implementation. No document found says whether the municipality's report on the canteen family was ever sent, whether the depot owner was compensated, or whether the land at the other sites was acquired. The evaluation review says the completion report does not report on compliance with the six policies.

title: Families moved off the Balakhani landfill and waste pickers who lost it

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P110679, ARP II Integrated Solid Waste Management Project. Loan 7549-AZ (IBRD-75490, US$29.5 million, agreement conformed 20 May 2009) and additional financing loan 8274-AZ (IBRD-82740, US$47.1 million, agreement 10 January 2014). Approved 17 June 2008, effective 31 July 2009, closed 31 August 2018 against an original closing date of 30 September 2013; US$76.6 million disbursed. The completion report of 28 February 2019 rates the overall outcome Satisfactory and the social safeguards performance Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's assessment of 13 September 2021 was a field-based Project Performance Assessment Report.

companies.name: Tamiz Shahar JSC
companies.role: The state joint-stock company that took full ownership and management of the Balakhani landfill on 14 October 2009, ran its rehabilitation, and later operated the materials recovery facility and the waste-to-energy plant. The resettlement plan uses that date as the cut-off for establishing who was affected.

community: Six families lived on the Balakhani landfill from 1993 to 2009. The resettlement action plan of May 2011 says they have 14 members in total, that they first lived in tents and picked waste, and that they built housing as they earned. It says they bought a shredder in 2004 and built a workshop, bought a second shredder and a washing line in 2006 and built a second workshop, and kept pigs fed on the waste in sheds made from waste materials. The plan says they had no legal claim to the land, which has been designated for landfilling since 1963 and which it describes as severely polluted by municipal, medical and at times hazardous waste. Before the plan was written the residents wrote complaint letters to senior ministers, to government agencies and to the Bank. The plan says: "The letters resulted in an escalation of grievance between all stakeholders in the project and the eventual awarding of a court order to TS JSC supporting the forcible eviction of the PAP. On the insistence of the World Bank and all Government stakeholders the court order was never enacted." It describes the residents' main grievance as a mistaken belief, "borne from miscommunication and misunderstanding", that they would be moved without compensation, and says the plan process had restored harmonious relations. The project also affected people who did not live on the site but earned a living picking waste there. The completion report of 28 February 2019 counts 144 project-affected people in a 2011 survey, including the six families. It says those living on the site were offered apartments in Baku and those whose livelihoods were affected were offered employment, that "Most continued employment either safely at the landfill, or with Tamiz Shahar in the sorting facility with benefits, including pension", that all employees and registered waste pickers were given helmets, gloves and other clothing, and that Tamiz Shahar held 30 individual meetings with waste pickers between September 2014 and February 2015. It notes the project won the Bank's Europe and Central Asia Vice-Presidential Award in 2014, partly for the way the government engaged with the waste pickers. The Independent Evaluation Group's field assessment of 13 September 2021 gives a different count of what happened to them. It says "Six families living at the landfill site were provided with new housing", and then: "However, only 14 of the 100 to 110 waste pickers accepted Tamiz Shahar JSC's proposal and began to work at the facility. Waste pickers reportedly stated that adhering to the eight-hour workday did not suit their preferences." It continues, in a sentence broken by a page break in the report, that currently, as confirmed by the Independent Evaluation Group mission, "only 11 waste pickers from those who were waste picking before the landfill rehabilitation are working at the Balakhani material recovery facility as employees of Tamiz Shahar JSC". It also says some preferred to keep picking at the landfill, that this is allowed under registration and monitoring with safety equipment in place, and that Tamiz Shahar pays waste pickers for plastic, glass and paper collected at the site.
outcome: The landfill was rehabilitated into a sanitary landfill with 20 years of capacity and the project closed in August 2018 having spent US$76.6 million. The six families were given new housing. Of the 100 to 110 waste pickers the Evaluation Group counted, 14 took jobs at the materials recovery facility and 11 were still working there when its mission visited in 2021. Picking at the landfill continues under registration.

title: 115 People Left Unpaid on Burundi's Fibre Backbone
place: Burundi's national fibre backbone, Bujumbura, Burundi

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Regional Communications Infrastructure Project, first phase (P094103), approved 29 March 2007. The Burundi grant closed on 31 October 2014, 27 months behind schedule; the three-country operation closed on 31 December 2016, after nine level two restructurings across the three countries. Burundi's share was Grant H283-BI, estimated at US$20.10 million at appraisal, with US$20.60 million disbursed, inside a three-country operation covering Burundi, Kenya and Madagascar whose grant estimate rose from US$164.5 million to US$249.6 million. The three countries contributed nothing of the US$37.40 million expected of them. The Evaluation Group rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory.

companies.name: Burundi Backbone System (BBS)
companies.role: The company that built and ran the national fibre network under the project; the state revoked its public-private status and nationalised it in January 2017

community: The project laid 1,254 km of fibre optic cable across Burundi, reaching 34 communes, and linked 58 government institutions and 14 universities. The Evaluation Group's review of the completion report says that in Burundi "compensations were paid in full for 8,265 people for a total amount of Burundian Franc (BIF) 105,311,800 (equivalent of approximately US$67,000 in April 2015)", and that "115 people were yet to be paid compensation at project closure". The documents do not say what the 8,265 people lost, do not break the sum down, and do not say why the 115 were not paid. In Kenya the review says no resettlement was needed. In Madagascar compensation was paid in full, US$56,941 under the resettlement plan and US$9,241 under the environmental and social management plan; the resettlement plan of July 2012 for zones 1A and 2 covers four affected people at four of the 68 sites, with a budget of 43,562,500 ariary, and records that at one site only two households were involved so the survey results did not have to be posted publicly.
outcome: The network was working when the project closed. The review records that the authorities revoked the public-private status of Burundi Backbone System and nationalised it in January 2017, "without consultation or compensation", officially on the grounds that the shareholders were not respecting their contractual terms, and rates the sustainability risk Significant for that reason. No document says whether the 115 people were ever paid.

title: Land acquired from the Takon community for the Porto-Novo landfill, compensated in buildings and services
place: Takon, Sakété, Plateau department, near Porto-Novo, Benin

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Second Decentralized City Management Project, known as PGUD2 (P082725), IDA credit 4117-BJ of SDR 24.0 million (US$35.0 million equivalent) and an additional financing credit 4490-BJ of SDR 24.3 million (US$40.0 million equivalent); Board approval 12 September 2005, closing 29 June 2012 against an original date of 30 June 2010 (completion report ICR2504, 27 December 2012; evaluation review ICRR14151, 16 September 2013). Category B, triggering the Bank’s policies on environmental assessment and involuntary resettlement. The completion report rates the overall project outcome Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory. In July 2011 the Bank raised its disbursement percentage retroactively so unused funds could pay contractor invoices the government could no longer cover.

companies.name: Agence d’Exécution des Travaux Urbains (AGETUR)
companies.role: Benin’s urban works execution agency, a party to the project agreement for credit 4117-BJ and, with SERHAU, one of the two agencies that had run the first phase of the programme and carried out its environmental and social work

companies.name: Société d’Études Régionales d’Habitat et d’Aménagement Urbain (SERHAU)
companies.role: The other implementing agency named in the completion report for the programme’s first phase, and a supervisor of the environmental and social management plans under the second

community: The completion report says the government had to spend money it had set aside for its own share of the project on “unforeseen social measures that needed to be taken during the resettlement of communities living near the Takon landfill”. Those measures were three classroom blocks, eight toilets, roads, clinics, a community centre, electricity and a small-scale water supply, amounting to CFA 830 million, and the report says they were supplied to compensate communities whose land was taken to build the landfill at Takon, near Porto-Novo. Because that money went on the compensation, the government could not meet its 10 per cent share of the original credit or its 15 per cent share of the additional financing, and in July 2011 asked for funds to be reallocated. The Independent Evaluation Group’s review gives the same account and adds that the landfill was not operating when the project closed: delays at the National Board for Procurement Control meant the operator’s contract was not signed until six months after the closing date. A footnote in the completion report records that resettlement was not planned during the programme’s first phase, but “some resettlement activity took place without a resettlement framework being in place”. Both documents say the project complied with all safeguard requirements, that resettlement action plans were prepared and carried out before civil works began, and that the Benin Environment Agency certified the works; the completion report rates safeguards satisfactory.
outcome: The communities received the buildings and services rather than cash. The landfill they gave up land for was still not being exploited at project closure, the operator’s contract being signed six months after the closing date; the Independent Evaluation Group’s review says the landfill was “still not fully functional by project closure”.

title: Road corridor works begun before compensation was finished in Burkina Faso, with seven households resettled in Mali
place: Ouagadougou to Sakoinsé section of National Road 1, Burkina Faso, on the Tema to Ouagadougou to Bamako corridor

lenders.name: World Bank (International Development Association)
lenders.role: Project P079749, West Africa Regional Transport and Transit Facilitation Project. IDA Credits 44350 (Mali), 44380 (Burkina Faso) and 44390 (Ghana), original commitment SDR 116.70 million, revised SDR 116.00 million, of which SDR 115.43 million was disbursed. Approved 19 June 2008, closing date 30 June 2015 (completion report ICR00003592, 31 December 2015; Financing Agreements for Credit 4438-BF conformed 8 July 2008, Credit 4439-GH conformed 11 July 2008 and Credit 4435-ML conformed 17 July 2008). Environmental category B. Two safeguard policies were triggered: Environmental Assessment (OP/BP/GP 4.01) and Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12); the Evaluation Group's assessment report says the second was triggered only for minor land acquisition or loss of income from the road rehabilitation or the construction of the rest stops. The completion report rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, risk to development outcome Moderate, Bank performance Satisfactory and borrower performance Moderately Satisfactory. The Evaluation Group's field-based assessment report of 19 April 2018 rates borrower performance moderately satisfactory and says the supervision of safeguards was satisfactory. Parallel financing came from the African Development Bank, the European Union and the West African Development Bank.

companies.name: Ministère des Infrastructures, des Transports et de l'Habitat, Burkina Faso
companies.role: The ministry whose directorate general of roads held the Burkina Faso works, applied the delay penalty clause to the Ouagadougou to Sakoinsé contractor and was responsible for the compensation plan for that section.

companies.name: Ministère de l'Équipement et des Transports, Mali
companies.role: The ministry that published the compensation and resettlement framework for the Malian sections of the corridor and held the Bamako to Bougouni and Sikasso to Hérémakono works.

companies.name: Ghana Highway Authority
companies.role: The roads agency, under Ghana's transport ministry, responsible for the Ghanaian corridor works and the land acquisition for the rest stops.

community: The credits rehabilitated road sections on the corridor from the port of Tema in Ghana through Ouagadougou to Bamako, and were to build rest stops. The completion report says that "the compensations were fully carried out, albeit with delays. Particularly in Burkina Faso, the works contract was signed while the compensations were still ongoing." In Ghana an increase in the financing let the resettlement and compensation, first budgeted from government funds, be paid faster. "In the case of Mali, involuntary resettlements were made for seven households. The compensations were fully financed from the counterpart funding resources." The Evaluation Group's field-based assessment report says all compensation payments were made, with delays in Burkina Faso and Ghana caused by government budget limits, that in Mali seven households were resettled and compensation was timely, and that "no information was obtained on how many people were compensated in Burkina Faso and Ghana". It names slow land acquisition in Ghana for the rest stops as the only shortcoming of the safeguards work. The abbreviated compensation plan for the Ouagadougou to Sakoinsé section, written in October 2007, names four people losing a hectare of land each and 800 kilogrammes of harvest a year at borrow pit 4 and at Douré and Sakoinsé, and lists trees lost at two other borrow pits. The borrower's own report, printed as an annex to the completion report, lists delays in payment of compensation and counterpart funds, and land acquisition, among the project's challenges.
outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2015. Both the completion report and the assessment report record all the compensation as eventually paid. The transit facilitation part of the project failed: the three countries never agreed on the customs arrangements.

title: Twenty Dangriga Market Vendors Were Moved Out for Twenty-Six Months and Lost a Quarter of Their Income
place: The Dangriga Municipal Market, Dangriga, Stann Creek District, Belize

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Belize Municipal Development Project (P111928), Loan 7958-BZ, fifteen million dollars, loan agreement dated 2 December 2010 with Belize. The evaluation review of 5 September 2017 gives the count: "Eight of the Bank's ten safeguard policies were triggered. They were Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01), Natural Habitats (OP/BP 4.04), Forests (OP/BP 4.36), Physical Cultural Resources (OP/BP 4.11), Indigenous Peoples (OP/BP 4.10), Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), Projects in Disputed Areas (OP/BP 7.60) and Projects on International Waterways (OP/BP 7.50)." The completion report of 5 June 2017 gives the indigenous peoples policy the number OP/BP 4.11 in its social safeguards paragraph, which is the number of the physical cultural resources policy. Both documents rate the outcome Satisfactory; the report rates the risk to the development outcome Moderate and the review rates it Modest. The report says "Four sites required development of Resettlement Plans. All vendors were resettled and moved to more lucrative locations, or compensated", and rates compliance with the social safeguard policies Satisfactory. The review drops the last three words of that sentence and reports it as "all vendors were resettled and moved to more lucrative locations", and adds that "The Bank project team confirmed to IEG that compliance with all safeguards was achieved for all subprojects by the end of the project", which is a staff statement and not a document. Neither the report nor the review mentions the income loss that the project's own abbreviated action plan of 20 August 2014 records. The total cost of the market sub-project is given in that plan as 1,519,364.33 Belize dollars, of which 1,475,111.00 from the World Bank loan and 44,253.33, three per cent, from the Dangriga Town Council.

companies.name: Belize Social Investment Fund
companies.role: The statutory fund that ran the project through its Project Implementation Unit, carried out the two evaluations of the vendors' losses and prepared the abbreviated action plan. The plan says the first contractor's works contract was terminated prematurely in September 2013. Channel 5 Belize reported on 30 January 2014 that work stopped amid allegations of an incompetent contractor and corruption at the fund, and Amandala reported on 4 April 2014 that four fund employees were dismissed after the first contractor alleged extortion in September 2013, and that the employees denied the claims.

companies.name: Dangriga Town Council
companies.role: The town council, which sought the funding to expand the market, put up three per cent of the sub-project cost, housed the displaced cooked-food and meat vendors in the renovated slaughterhouse and paid their utilities there, and operates the one-stall-per-family policy that the plan says affects five families, who are to be compensated with temporary stalls beside the Cubanos area. The plan says the council agreed to meet 14,990.68 Belize dollars of utility costs and 24,530.00 in stall-fee arrears for all the temporarily relocated vendors.

companies.name: K & G Construction
companies.role: The first contractor on the market works, whose principal the plan names as Mr Smart and whom Amandala names as Kenard Smart. The plan says his contract was terminated prematurely in September 2013 after works that had run from June 2012, and that during his tenure job openings for Dangriga residents were very limited, with more than 75 per cent of workers coming from outside the Stann Creek District. Channel 5 Belize reported on 23 October 2014 that he had been paid about 800,000 Belize dollars before work stopped.

companies.name: CB Construction
companies.role: The second contractor, of San Ignacio in the Cayo District, which took over the works. Amandala reported on 4 April 2014 that the contract was signed on 24 March 2014 for 1,228,310.95 Belize dollars with a pledge to finish in six months. The plan says civil works resumed in April 2014, and that in July 2014 about 12 of a workforce of 17 were Dangriga residents.

companies.name: Anthony Thurton & Associates
companies.role: The engineering consultancy that completed the final drawings and designs for the new market extension, which was to hold 22 new stalls with metal shutters (abbreviated action plan, 20 August 2014).

community:
To rebuild and extend the Dangriga municipal market, the main market building was emptied. The abbreviated action plan of 20 August 2014 says a joint decision was taken to vacate it during the works because heavy equipment was operating next to vendors and the buying public. Those moved out were the stall owners inside the market, those under the market awnings, those in the fish section and those between the market and the Cubanos area.

Then the works stopped. The plan says the first contractor's contract was terminated prematurely in September 2013 and the civil works did not resume until April 2014, a seven-month gap. A second evaluation was carried out with the vendors who had been moved, to see whether they were losing income because of the delay. Its result: "Initially, a total of twenty (20) vendors were temporarily relocated but this number was reduced to twelve (12) by July 2014 with the majority of them relocating to other locations of the municipality where they are more visible to the buying public. The results of the second evaluation are that on an average, the vendors were experiencing income losses of 25%." The plan's own table gives the length of relocation for those 20 as 26 months, and marks each of their losses moderate.

The first evaluation, reported in April 2011, had concluded that most of the stall owners who would be moved "would not be experiencing any major loss of income sources or means of livelihood".

On 30 January 2014, while the works were still stopped, Channel 5 Belize reported Mayor Gilbert Swaso saying that vendors had lost about 25 per cent of their income while the market was closed, and that the community had lost its market. The same report said the shortfall of about 450,000 Belize dollars needed to finish the market would be taken from a 1.5 million dollar allocation for road works in Dangriga's phase two, money the mayor said would otherwise have paved about 1.2 miles of streets that residents had chosen.

What the vendors received is set out in the plan. The cooked-food and meat vendors were housed inside the renovated slaughterhouse, with running water and electricity paid for by the town council. The fish, fruit and vegetable vendors got temporary stalls beside the slaughterhouse, with some protection from the weather but responsibility for the security of their own goods overnight. Those who had traded between the market and the Cubanos area went to a temporary site pending a permanent one under a second phase. The council agreed to cover 14,990.68 Belize dollars of utilities and 24,530.00 in stall-fee arrears for all the temporarily relocated vendors for July 2012 to September 2014. At its August 2014 meeting the project steering committee approved reimbursements of stall fees to four of the relocated vendors, 6,955.00 Belize dollars in all, for July 2012 to April 2014.

The parking lot, where a large number of vendors had put up make-shift stalls, was to be taken back and the vendors moved into a new extension holding at most 22 stalls, one per family. The plan says five families are affected by that policy and names them: Zepeda, Carillo, Segura, Arzu and Sho. In the same paragraph it says temporary stalls will be erected beside the Cubanos area for those parking-lot vendors "who will be compensated with one or more stalls lost as a result of the Town Council’s one stall per family policy", and its table values the loss of the four parking-lot stall owners it names at one stall each and the loss of the other sixteen in the parking lot at none. A census of all the stall owners found that 56 per cent were women, that 70 per cent were of Mestizo ancestry in a town about 75 per cent of whose people are Garifuna, that 70 per cent paid between 15 and 22 Belize dollars a week for their stalls, and that weekly earnings ranged from 300 to 1,000 dollars in the parking lot to 900 to 3,000 dollars under the awnings. Fourteen sets of consultations were held with the vendors between April 2011 and July 2014.
outcome: The renovated market opened on 23 October 2014, Channel 5 Belize reported, after works that began in June 2012, with 44 stalls. The report gives the cost as 1,843,419.67 Belize dollars, above budget, with the first contractor paid about 800,000 before work stopped and the second contract costing roughly a million more. It quotes Mayor Swaso saying the building still lacked modern amenities and that some defects would be rectified, and says a government minister apologised to Dangriga residents for the delays. The project itself closed on 30 November 2016. The World Bank's completion report of 5 June 2017 says "All vendors were resettled and moved to more lucrative locations, or compensated", and rates compliance with the social safeguard policies Satisfactory; neither it nor the evaluation review mentions the 25 per cent income loss the project's own action plan records.

title: Land Taken for El Alto's Avenues and Paid For Years Afterwards
place: Avenida Santa Vera Cruz in Districts 5 and 6 and Avenida Litoral in the Urbanización El Paraíso, El Alto, Bolivia

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Credits IDA-42470 (4247-BO) and IDA-51680 (5168-BO) for the Bolivia Urban Infrastructure Project (P083979). US$54,000,000 in all, US$30,000,000 under the first credit and US$24,000,000 under the additional financing, of which US$46,218,927 was disbursed. Borrower the Plurinational State of Bolivia. Approved 21 November 2006, effective 12 September 2007, mid-term review 25 September 2009, original closing 30 November 2010, actual closing 30 September 2017, after restructurings beginning 15 August 2010. Component 1 upgraded neighbourhoods in La Paz, Component 2 urban transport in El Alto and Component 3 sewerage in Santa Cruz. Involuntary Resettlement (OP/BP 4.12), Environmental Assessment (OP/BP 4.01) and Physical Cultural Resources (OP/BP 4.11) were triggered; the appraisal document said no resettlement was expected but that works under Components 1 and 2 might in very limited cases entail population displacement. The completion report, dated 26 March 2018, rated outcome Moderately Satisfactory, Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory and monitoring and evaluation Modest, and rated compliance with environmental safeguards Satisfactory. The Independent Evaluation Group's review ICRR0021219 gave the same ratings with no disagreement recorded and rated the quality of the completion report Substantial.

companies.name: Gobierno Autónomo Municipal de El Alto
companies.role: The municipality that carried out the El Alto urban transport component. The completion report records that it prepared a conflict management plan and said that documentation of a "voluntary cession of land" had been planned before the project identification phase but was carried out after the Bank became involved, and that it then prepared an abbreviated resettlement plan for retroactive, in-kind compensation. It is left in charge of the one case unresolved at closing (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 March 2018).

companies.name: Gobierno Autónomo Municipal de La Paz
companies.role: The municipality that ran the neighbourhood upgrading component under its Programa Barrios de Verdad. The completion report records that all adverse impacts on third parties in La Paz were dealt with by changes in design, repositioning front walls and small structures such as stairs at the entrances of houses, and that the city prepared an abbreviated resettlement plan establishing in-kind replacement of perimeter walls, entrance stairs and railings (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 26 March 2018).

community:
The project paved avenues in El Alto, upgraded poor neighbourhoods in La Paz and extended sewerage in Santa Cruz.

On the El Alto avenues the land had already been handed over before the Bank arrived. The completion report says the municipality "prepared a Conflict Management Plan and indicated that documentation of a 'voluntary cession of land' had been planned before the PP's identification phase, but had been carried out after the Bank's involvement in project identification". The municipality then prepared an abbreviated resettlement plan "to provide retroactive, in-kind compensation to 6 property owners for the land they had ceded for the construction of 'Av. Santa Vera Cruz - Tramo 1'. Five of the six cases were solved at the end of the Project, and property owners obtained legal titles for their lots (with their new square footage). Only one case is pending", left with the El Alto municipal government, which expected to finish it within a couple of months.

The retroactive plan for Avenida Litoral, dated 10 November 2010, describes the same pattern on another avenue. Eleven residents of the Urbanización El Paraíso, named one by one in the plan, ceded the land needed for a road line of 48.5 metres, which the municipality had fixed in 2003, two years before the Bank's first identification mission in April 2005. The municipality had itself given up part of the municipal right of way, reducing the line from the 60 metres the law set for a first-order road to 48.5 metres, to avoid expropriating more of the residents' plots; even at 48.5 metres the plots were still encroaching on the right of way by an average of 11.5 square metres. All eleven plots were partially affected and none wholly, and the plan's table of affected assets carries the note that no valuation is made because the transfer is a return of municipal land. Two further signatories of the 2003 agreement, in block M, were held not to be affected at all, because their plans had been approved respecting the 48.5-metre line, so what they had declared as voluntarily ceded was in the plan's words a return of municipal property they had encroached on. Because the areas ceded came to more than 10 per cent of each plot, the Bank's policy required retroactive compensation, and the plan says the Bank was examining whether the 2003 agreement had legal force, whether its signatories were still the owners, and whether they still agreed with what they had signed, since "the areas ceded by the residents are greater than 10%, which may imply an impact of great magnitude for the owners". Of the eleven signatories, the plan notes, one had died, one was a new owner, and for one the original title documents were missing and that owner's willingness to sign the updated agreement had still to be established. The municipality's own position in the same plan is that the safeguards were not triggered, because its legal acts with third parties predate its commitments to the Bank; it would nonetheless make "some compensations" to the eleven, in the form of legalising their title and improving their basic services, and the plan's schedule prices those at 40,876.11 bolivianos in all.

The abbreviated resettlement plan for Avenida Santa Vera Cruz, dated July 2013, counted 137 properties built over the municipal line. One hundred and twenty-eight of them encroached on part of the pavement without blocking it and were not treated as affected; nine blocked the pavement and part of the carriageway and had to pull back to the line. One of the nine owners waived the entitlement and said he would move back at his own expense, leaving eight eligible. In every case the loss was partial and nobody had to move elsewhere. The plan also counted the trades along the avenue: 44 shops selling building materials and daily food, and 54 vehicles belonging to hauliers carrying sand, stone and building materials. Neither group was to get any material compensation. The shops were promised crossings so customers could still reach them; the hauliers were promised help in moving to a nearby part of the avenue where they could work in much the same way.
outcome: The credits closed on 30 September 2017, nearly seven years after the original closing date, with US$46.2 million of US$54 million disbursed. Five of the six owners on Avenida Santa Vera Cruz Tramo 1 had been compensated in kind and held legal title to their plots at their new size. One case was unresolved and left with the El Alto municipal government, which expected to close it within a couple of months. The completion report credits a community development strategy and a grievance redress service in El Alto with building a stable relationship between the project agencies and the residents and with the successful execution of the resettlement plan. The completion report rated the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

title: Seven Killed and Ninety-nine Properties Hit When the Pinheiros Station Works Collapsed
place: Rua Gilberto Sabino, Rua Capri, Rua Conselheiro Pereira Pinto, Rua Eugênio de Medeiros and Rua Amaro Cavalheiro, beside the Pinheiros station works on Metro Line 4, São Paulo, Brazil

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: The works where the ground collapsed were the civil works of Phase 1 of São Paulo Metro Line 4, which the Bank financed. The completion report for the Line 5 project, dated 22 June 2021, lists among the Bank's prior operations in the metropolitan region "the Metro Line 4 Phase 1 Project (P051696), approved in 2002", says those operations supported "construction of Phase 1 of Line 4", and records that "Line 4 Phase 1 was financed under World Bank procurement guidelines". That is the opposite of the arrangement on Line 5, whose appraisal document says the civil works "will be financed and executed by the Borrower" and that construction accident risk "is an indirect risk because Bank is not involved in the civil works". The resettlement plan for the accident is disclosed in the Bank's document archive as RP591, filed under the São Paulo Metro Line 4 Project Additional Financing (P105959), whose approval ICIJ's table records as 8 April 2008, fifteen months after the collapse; the archive files the additional financing's own project paper of 3 March 2008 under both that number and P051696. No completion report and no evaluation review filed under the additional financing number could be reached, and no Bank document found for it states a loan number or an amount. The appraisal document for the São Paulo Metro Line 5 Project (P116170), dated 3 March 2010, records that the State of São Paulo had been managing Metro Line 4 Phases 1 and 2 as a Bank Category A project requiring Environmental Assessment and Involuntary Resettlement policies, that "during project implementation of Line 4 (Phase 1) in January 2007, an accident occurred in which 7 people died due to the collapse of the tunnel at Pinheiros station which was being excavated", and that this "led to additional involuntary resettlement due to damage to homes and to the need to evacuate other dwellings and businesses until their safety could be assured". The same document says the Bank reviewed the design and implementation of the required resettlement and found it satisfactory, and that "the resettlement and compensation of affected parties is now complete, with no cases pending". It also lists the lessons of the Pinheiros accident among the measures to be taken into account on Line 5.

companies.name: Consórcio Via Amarela
companies.role: The consortium carrying out the Line 4 civil works at the Pinheiros station site when the ground collapsed. The resettlement plan says the people and families affected by the accident continued to be dealt with by this consortium and by the São Paulo Metrô, and that the consortium reported the dates on which displaced residents left their hotels or other lodgings (Plano de Reassentamento, December 2007).

companies.name: Companhia do Metropolitano de São Paulo (Metrô)
companies.role: The state metro company building Line 4-Amarela, which ran the census of the affected population and the monitoring visits to resettled households, and which the São Paulo state court ordered to be reimbursed R$6.5 million, the value of the contract, in the improbity judgment published on 16 February 2024 (Plano de Reassentamento, December 2007; Tribunal de Justiça de São Paulo notice, 16 February 2024).

companies.name: Prefeitura Municipal de São Paulo
companies.role: The city government, whose structural reports on the damaged buildings decided which of them could be reoccupied. The plan's table of property conditions distinguishes 34 properties released with a city report, 10 released with reservations, 11 released quickly as minimal impact and 3 with no city intervention (Plano de Reassentamento, December 2007).

community:
On 12 January 2007 the ground gave way at the works for the future Pinheiros station of Line 4-Amarela of the São Paulo metro. Seven people were killed. A resettlement plan setting out the position as at 31 October 2007, published in December 2007 by the metro company and disclosed in the World Bank's archive as RP591 under the Line 4 additional financing, records what the accident did to the neighbourhood. The plan itself names no lender.

Ninety-nine properties were affected, on five streets: 42 on Rua Gilberto Sabino, 30 on Rua Capri, 18 on Rua Conselheiro Pereira Pinto, 7 on Rua Eugênio de Medeiros and 2 on Rua Amaro Cavalheiro. Fifty-eight were residential, 25 commercial, 6 mixed with work carried on at home, 9 unoccupied and 1 other. Twelve were condemned and six demolished; six were sealed off, 17 were still under analysis, 34 were released with a city structural report, 10 released with reservations, 11 released quickly as minimal impact and 3 had no city intervention.

Two hundred and seventy-one people were affected, not counting the owners who did not live in the properties, of whom there were 57. The census counted 134 women and 137 men, 42 people over 65, 52 with chronic illness and 2 with disabilities. Forty-three of the households were tenants paying rent, 10 occupied properties lent to them, 36 were resident owners and one entry is recorded as squatters.

Seven deaths are recorded. Eight indemnity agreements were signed for them, because in one case the victim had two families.

Of the 99 properties, nine were empty on the day of the accident and four stayed occupied with minimal impact. Eighty cases had been settled by 31 October 2007, producing 34 returns to the original property, 59 resettlement addresses and 8 atypical cases with neither a return nor a resettlement; the plan notes that some occupants split between several addresses after resettlement. Six cases were still awaiting negotiation: three families lodged only in hotels, one split between a hotel and a relative's house, and two lodged with relatives with their cases in litigation. The hotels used were the George V, the Golden Tower and the New Citi. By the end of October 2007, 103 agreements had been signed out of 147 cases, three of them that month, with 30.67 per cent of those affected back in their own property and 53.15 per cent moved to another; the plan notes that one case can produce more than one agreement. The agreements signed covered indemnity for death, moral and material damages, material damages, damages for the dissolution of a tenancy, lost profits together with moral and material damages, lost profits with other indemnities, and other indemnities.

On 16 February 2024 the São Paulo state court published a first-instance decision in case 0009559-70.2010.8.26.0053, given by the 5th Public Treasury Court of the state capital, holding six people and seven companies liable for administrative improbity over the collapse. The six lost any public office they held, had their political rights suspended for five years, were fined at twice the damage, which is to be quantified later, and were barred for five years from contracting with the public sector or receiving public benefits or tax incentives; the seven companies were fined on the same basis and barred on the same terms. The court ordered the defendants to reimburse the São Paulo Metrô R$6.5 million, the value of the contract, along with what it had spent on indemnities, legal fees and costs, and to pay R$232 million in collective moral damages and R$1.2 million in diffuse property damages. On causation the judge wrote that "as perfurações foram executadas no local já fragilizado, e os suportes de sustentação previstos não foram colocados de imediato" — the drilling was done at a spot already weakened and the planned supports were not put in at once — and found the conduct negligent and the site plainly exposed to imminent risk of collapse, the drilling having been done to get ahead of schedule. He found that representatives of the Metrô had abandoned their duty to supervise and that the consortium's experts had taken no immediate or deeper analysis of the instability they knew of. The decision can be appealed. The court's notice names neither the individuals nor the companies.
outcome: The resettlement plan's position at 31 October 2007 was 80 of 99 cases settled and six still in negotiation, two of those in litigation. The appraisal document for Line 5, dated 3 March 2010, says the resettlement and compensation of the affected parties was complete with no cases pending, and that the Bank had reviewed the design and implementation of the resettlement and found it satisfactory. The São Paulo state court's improbity judgment of February 2024, seventeen years after the collapse, holds six people and seven companies liable, orders R$6.5 million reimbursed to the metro company, R$232 million in collective moral damages and R$1.2 million in diffuse property damages, and leaves the civil fines of twice the damage to be quantified later; it is subject to appeal.

companies.name: Municipality of Santos Secretariat of Government
companies.role: The implementing agency named in the completion report's data sheet. The Secretariat of Government, with support from COHAB-Santos under a specific agreement, took on the institutional responsibilities for resettlement. All resettlement activities were to be paid for out of the municipality's own counterpart funds, not the loan (Implementation Completion and Results Report, 7 June 2016).

community:
The project was meant to clear and upgrade stilt-house settlements on the Río dos Bugres in the northwest of Santos. The appraisal document of 29 October 2009 said about 2,400 families lived in those slums and about 1,100 of them, living in stilt houses, would be resettled into new houses.

By the time the loan closed on 30 June 2015, 712 families had been resettled: 480 to the Vila Pelé II housing complex in 2012, 160 to Caneleira IV Phase 1 in 2014 and 72 to Quadras 1 and 35 in Vila Gilda in 2014. The completion report puts that at 54 per cent of the number estimated in the resettlement action plan. Its resettlement summary table lists 1,324 housing units in total, 712 delivered by the end of the project and 612 still to come, including 520 at Caneleira IV Phase 2 then under construction. A further 88 families, in Vila Gilda, received improved water and sanitation services and adjustments to their housing conditions rather than a move. The project's own indicator was a package of municipal services for 2,400 households; 800 were reached.

In October 2011 the municipality told the Bank it had found 65 more affected families living in the works area, and agreed to pay for temporary housing until they could be moved to new houses, then planned for 2013. At a supervision mission in May 2012 the Bank team found that those families had instead been moved into other stilt houses, built by the municipality, "disregarding the RAP terms and the Bank Policies". The Bank demanded immediate action and the families were moved into temporary housing on housing allowances. The completion report states that by the end of the project "the 65 families, referred above, had not been properly resettled". Annex 4 says around 40 of them reached Caneleira IV Phase 1 late in 2015 and that in May 2016 the municipality confirmed 23 more had finally been resettled, to Caneleira IV Phase 2. Three households were still waiting, with the municipality saying it meant to move them in the second half of 2016. The footnote to the report's resettlement summary table describes a group of the same size and destination differently: "Twenty-three families from Caminho São José (that were receiving rent allowance by EOP) were resettled at Canaleira IV (2nd Phase) in the first half of 2016. The remaining 3 families are supposed to be resettled along the 2nd half of 2016." One account puts the 23 in the group of 65 and the other at Caminho São José, and the report does not say whether they are the same households.

Three expropriation authorisations for the macro-drainage works were still outstanding at closing. The Bank asked in 2015 for an abbreviated resettlement plan for around 30 families occupying pumping station work sites and rejected the one submitted for not complying with its policy; the works were then suspended. A study finished in October 2015, after the project closed, recommended removing the stilt houses within 50 metres of the EEC7 pumping station and within 20 metres of the others. The completion report says the municipality has not yet estimated how many families that is. Geotechnical experts also found that excavation for part of the EEC7 culvert could cause structural damage to nearby buildings.

The completion report records that the 712 families moved from precarious stilt houses into apartment buildings and that the resettlement produced noticeable effects on poverty. None of the Phase I macro-drainage works were finished, so the project achieved little or no flood protection.
outcome: The loan closed on 30 June 2015 with US$24.51 million of US$44.00 million disbursed. Of the 1,324 housing units in the completion report's table, 612 were still to be delivered after closing. Three households from the group of 65 were still waiting to be moved when the report was written, and the Bank said it was continuing to follow up. The macro-drainage works were suspended, and the Bank told the municipality that all outstanding resettlement and expropriation matters had to be resolved under the resettlement action plan and its safeguard policy before any of the macro-drainage works could continue. Post-occupation surveys reported in the report's economic annex confirm that the resettled population was satisfied with the new condition, and the report records that the 712 families moved into housing complexes with electricity, water supply and wastewater piping. The completion report rated the outcome Unsatisfactory and the Independent Evaluation Group agreed.

title: Structures and businesses lost to land pooling in Thimphu, with three owners never traced or paid
place: Dechencholing, Lanjopakha and Taba local area plans, Thimphu, Bhutan

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Second Bhutan Urban Development Project, project number P090157, credit IDA-47440 of US$12.0 million approved 29 April 2010, with additional credit IDA-54310 of US$17.4 million; effective 24 August 2010, closing extended from 31 December 2015 to 30 June 2019; US$24.8 million disbursed of US$29.4 million. The completion report of 27 December 2019 rates social safeguard compliance Satisfactory (paragraph 67); the Independent Evaluation Group reviewed it on 16 March 2020.

companies.name: Thimphu Thromde
companies.role: Implementing agency named in the completion report, alongside the Ministry of Works and Human Settlements. Thimphu's municipal corporation; its Urban Planning Division ran the social impact work and its Social Development and Resettlement Cell, which the completion report says the city could not fully staff, handled resettlement. The unpaid compensation sits in the Thromde's accounts section. No construction contractor is named in the documents.

community: The project serviced three new neighbourhoods in Thimphu by land pooling: landowners kept their plots but gave up a share of their land for roads and services instead of the state buying it outright. The Independent Evaluation Group's review, citing page 66 of the appraisal document, says all project-affected title owners who had agreed to the approach and to contributing 25 per cent of their land were to receive compensation for structures, other assets and livelihood plus resettlement assistance; that is the plan, not an outcome. The completion report lists what people lost: physical structures, fruit trees, businesses and access to rental houses because of the land pooling, and temporary restrictions on agricultural land where water mains were laid. Neither document counts the structures or the households. A footnote to the completion report records that when the project ended only three affected households or persons were left to be paid, because they could not be tracked despite repeated efforts, and that their compensation has been kept in the Thromde's accounts section and is available for payment. A grievance committee met regularly on complaints about land pooling and compensation payments, and verified payments before they went up for approval. A beneficiary survey found that 60 per cent of residents in Dechencholing, 60 per cent in Lanjopakha and 54 per cent in Taba reported better quality of life since moving to the new neighbourhood.
outcome: The project closed on 30 June 2019. Three affected owners had still not been found or paid, and their money remained with Thimphu Thromde. The completion report presents the land pooling itself as a success, saying it cut the government's land acquisition and compensation costs and is now being asked for in other areas, such as the settlement of Kabesa next to Dechencholing.

title: A Family Moved and Five Fatal Accidents at Morupule B
place: Morupule B power station, near Palapye, Central District, Botswana

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Morupule B Generation and Transmission Project (P112516, also filed as P116784), IBRD loan 78010 of US$136.4 million and an IBRD partial credit guarantee of US$242.7 million, approved 29 October 2009, effective 9 August 2010; US$68.88 million of the loan was disbursed and nothing was paid under the guarantee. The loan did not pay for the power station: the completion report says the government asked for it "to help finance the facilities associated with the power plant - water supply and transmission lines - and some technical assistance and capacity building activities", while the plant itself was built under an US$825 million loan from the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, which the guarantee supported by extending its repayment period from 15 to 20 years. The report also records that the choice of technology and the selection of the engineering, procurement and construction contractor "were taken prior to the involvement of the World Bank", that the contract was signed in November 2008 and construction began on 29 April 2009, and that the Bank completed appraisal in August 2009. The power plant was nonetheless the central component of the Bank's project and the report calls it so. The loan closed on 30 June 2014 and the guarantee on 9 September 2015. The completion report rates the outcome, Bank performance and borrower performance all Unsatisfactory and the risk to the development outcome High (6 October 2016); the Evaluation Group agrees with all four ratings.

lenders.name: African Development Bank, Industrial and Commercial Bank of China and Sinosure
lenders.role: Co-financiers and partners named in the completion report's data sheet

companies.name: Botswana Power Corporation (BPC)
companies.role: State utility that built and runs the plant, handled the resettlement and the compensation on the transmission corridors, and was found by the lender's mission to be weak in enforcing safety standards

companies.name: China National Electronic Equipment Corporation (CNEEC)
companies.role: Named by the newspaper Mmegi as the main contractor at the plant. The World Bank's completion report refers only to "the EPC contractor" and does not name it

companies.name: NEPEC 11
companies.role: Named by Mmegi as a subcontractor at the plant; thirty of its workers said they were retrenched after stopping work over safety and pay

community: One family lived on the footprint of the power station: a woman of 97, her daughter, the daughter's husband and their granddaughter, with a grandson who lived in Palapye and visited. Their home was two small huts built mainly of scrap and found materials, a store and a fence, on about 2,000 square metres of yard and field. They had three donkeys and a donkey cart, which they used to fetch water from outside, and they lived on firewood, mopane worms and fruit they collected and sold in Palapye and on crops they grew for themselves. The abbreviated resettlement plan of May 2009 records that they did not plant their usual food crops that year because they knew they would be moved, and that they were to be compensated for that lost harvest. Two plots were cleared for them about 5 to 6 km from Palapye, each to get a house of 3.4 by 10 metres and a pit latrine; while that was built the family was housed in tents on the plots, and the plan says they were to be moved on 25 May 2009. The family asked to stay about the same distance from Palapye so they could keep travelling there daily and keep their way of living. The plan also records that neither grandchild had ever been to school, and that the husband had no identity card, had tried once to get one and lacked the witnesses he needed. On the transmission line corridors, the completion report records that compensation was paid to informal settlers, that one house had to be demolished with its owner relocated to a nearby town, that those works, including the well fields, had an impact on about 130 households, and that two landowners complained about the compensation terms and about a borehole being moved, both complaints being resolved. The Evaluation Group repeats all of it, and adds that "the project team confirmed a resettlement action plan was prepared and successfully implemented". Five fatal accidents happened at the plant: in February 2011, August 2011, September 2012, December 2013 and March 2015. All but the December 2013 accident were falls from height; that one the report puts down to poor coordination of repairs, and the March 2015 one was a fall from height during boiler repair work. The completion report says safety remained a serious concern throughout the project, with weaknesses in enforcing safety standards and procedures, a lax safety environment, and weak control of who entered and left the site for much of the construction. An action plan was agreed after the first accident and widened after the second, after which the lender's October 2011 mission "concluded that there was a serious lack of safety observance and enforcement at the site for which the main EPC contractor should take prime responsibility". Only after the third accident did the utility suspend work at height, tighten site security and hire both a safety supervision firm and a separate scaffolding contractor; police officers were deployed to enforce site security. The environment department and the waste management department made frequent site visits and fines were levied on the utility and the contractor for breaches over hygiene, waste disposal, sewage ponds, oil and acid storage and insufficient dust suppression. Noise in parts of the plant exceeded both the contract requirements and industry standards.
outcome: The plant was built but has run far below what was expected: it was meant to work at an annual capacity factor of about 80 per cent and has not. The completion report rates the project Unsatisfactory on outcome, on Bank performance and on borrower performance, and the risk to the development outcome High, and the Evaluation Group agrees. Emissions from the stacks were not measured reliably because the instruments malfunctioned or were not calibrated, and the report says sulphur oxide emissions were likely to have breached the standards whenever the limestone injection system broke down. Ambient air quality data only became available in August 2015, from a single monitoring station moved over from the older Morupule A plant.

title: Housing demolition for the Chunhu access road came to more than double the plan

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Project P106956, loan IBRD-78490 of US$50 million for the Ningbo New Countryside Development Project, approved 25 February 2010, effective 16 July 2010, closed 31 March 2016 with no restructuring; the full US$50 million was disbursed. Environmental category B. Three safeguard policies were triggered: environmental assessment OP 4.01, safety of dams OP 4.37 and involuntary resettlement OP 4.12. The Bank's completion report of 20 October 2016 rates the outcome Satisfactory, Bank performance Satisfactory, borrower performance Satisfactory and risk to the development outcome Moderate. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 13 February 2017 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, one notch lower. Its stated reason has five parts: relevance of objective High, relevance of design Substantial, achievement of the rural wastewater objective Substantial, achievement of the infrastructure objective Substantial, achievement of the objective of enhancing township management in small towns Modest, and efficiency Substantial. The review also rates Bank performance Moderately Satisfactory where the report rates it Satisfactory, and rates risk to the development outcome Substantial, naming risks it says materialised without being identified or mitigated; the report itself puts that risk at Moderate and the review's column for the report prints it as Modest. The review agrees with the report on borrower performance.

companies.name: Ningbo Municipality Development and Reform Commission
companies.role: Implementing agency. The completion report names it as the implementing agency; the Ningbo municipal project management office sat within it, with project implementation units in Fenghua, Ninghai and Yuyao counties. No construction contractor is named in the documents.

companies.name: Fenghua Investment Co., Ltd.
companies.role: The completion report names it as the project implementation unit for the Chunhu Town infrastructure development component, responsible for the design and construction of that infrastructure and for servicing the debt from asset management fees paid by Fenghua City. It is also named as the author of the June 2009 resettlement action plan for the Chunhu small town development sub-project. The Evaluation Group rates its performance Moderately Satisfactory.

community: The loan paid for rural wastewater treatment in 144 villages, a coastal water supply in Fenghua and town infrastructure at Chunhu, including the Fenghua to Chunhu access road. The Bank's completion report says that the permanent land acquisition and the demolition of houses both came out higher than planned. Its table in the social safeguards annex gives the finished figures against the planned ones: 325.63 mu of land permanently acquired against 265.06 planned, a rise the report puts at 24 per cent, and 7,647.6 square metres of housing demolished against 3,479 planned. All of the extra demolition is on the access road component, where 7,647.6 square metres came down against 3,027 planned; the report says the demolition doubled because of unforeseen requirements for that road, and that land first thought to need only temporary occupation had to be bought outright because it was unusable on its own once the parcels next to it had been taken. The report also says a grievance system was set up and no complaints were received over the life of the project, that all property losses were adequately compensated, and that a survey by outside monitors put the per capita net income of affected households at about RMB 58,600 in 2015 against about RMB 40,000 in 2009, with 44 per cent of affected people very satisfied with their living conditions, 50 per cent somewhat satisfied and just under 6 per cent neither satisfied nor dissatisfied.
outcome: The project closed on 31 March 2016. The completion report says the resettlement and the buying of the additional land were carried out satisfactorily in line with the resettlement plan, and that a post-evaluation by the National Research Center for Resettlement found the Bank's social safeguard requirements satisfactorily met. No Bank document found counts how many households lost the 7,647.6 square metres of housing.
